lineage_context.teaching_goal: Use absorptive peltate trichomes plus a 3+3 flower plan to connect epiphytic Tillandsia with terrestrial spinose Hechtia, then separate the two project genera by leaf margin, habit, flower sexuality, and seed architecture.

project_scope.selection_mode: Project module across Tillandsia recurvata, Tillandsia usneoides, and Hechtia texensis
project_scope.note: The project pool contains two epiphytic Tillandsia species and one terrestrial/lithophytic Hechtia. All three names remain accepted under current Kew.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with the leaf surface: Bromeliaceae nearly always bears specialized peltate trichomes/scales that absorb water. Then inspect the flower for two whorls of 3 perianth parts and 6 stamens.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Perennial herbs that may be epiphytic, terrestrial, or lithophytic. Leaves are simple and often arranged in rosettes or reduced stem systems; margins may be entire or spinose. Peltate absorptive trichomes are a major family character.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers usually have 3 sepals + 3 petals and 6 stamens. Ovary position varies across the family. Inflorescences often have conspicuous bracts.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Capsule or berry depending on lineage. Project Tillandsia makes capsules with plumose seed appendages; project Hechtia makes capsules with narrowly winged to nearly wingless seeds lacking plumose appendages.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Do not memorize bromeliads as 'pineapple-shaped.' The transferable family door is peltate water-absorbing trichomes + 3 sepals + 3 petals + 6 stamens.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: peltate trichome → 3+3 flower → Tillandsia epiphyte door → Hechtia terrestrial door → Tillandsia species silhouettes → grass/sedge/rush contrast
visual_lesson.intro: This family is a great visual reminder that Poales is much bigger than grasses. A gray air plant hanging from an oak and a spiny false-agave rosette share the same bromeliad flower plan and absorptive leaf-scale technology.

steps.title: 1 · Zoom into a bromeliad trichome
steps.look_for: Shieldlike peltate scales covering the leaf surface, often dense enough to make Tillandsia look gray or silver.
steps.why_it_matters: These scales absorb water and help explain how epiphytic bromeliads can live without rooting in soil.

steps.title: 2 · Count the flower in threes
steps.why_it_matters: Connects wildly different project growth forms through one reproductive plan.

steps.title: 3 · Tillandsia door: entire margins + epiphytic habit
steps.look_for: Usually epiphytic gray-scaled plant with entire leaf margins; bisexual flowers, superior ovary, capsule, and seeds with a basal white plumose appendage.
steps.why_it_matters: Separates the project Tillandsia lineage from spinose terrestrial Hechtia.

steps.title: 4 · Hechtia door: spiny terrestrial rosette
steps.photo_role: Hechtia texensis rosette + male/female flower comparison
steps.look_for: Terrestrial or rock-growing rosette with pungent spinose leaf margins; male and female flowers occur on different plants.
steps.why_it_matters: Hechtia looks superficially agave-like, but its bromeliad reproductive structure and family trichomes put it in Bromeliaceae.

steps.title: 5 · Ballmoss vs Spanish moss
steps.photo_role: Tillandsia recurvata vs T. usneoides silhouette
steps.look_for: T. recurvata forms compact ball-like clumps with short recurved leaves; T. usneoides forms long pendent festoons with very narrow gray-scaled leaves.
steps.why_it_matters: A whole-plant silhouette separates the two Hays-project Tillandsia species quickly.

steps.title: 6 · False agave is not an agave
steps.look_for: Hechtia has spinose bromeliad leaves plus separate male/female plants and small 3+3 flowers; Agave belongs to Asparagaceae and has a different reproductive architecture.
steps.why_it_matters: Prevents a very plausible rosette-based misidentification.

comparisons.title: Bromeliaceae vs Poaceae
comparisons.rule: Bromeliaceae has simple often rosette-forming leaves with absorptive peltate scales and ordinary 3+3 flowers; Poaceae has jointed culms, sheath/collar/ligule architecture and spikelets built from glumes, lemma and palea.

comparisons.title: Bromeliaceae vs Cyperaceae/Juncaceae
comparisons.rule: Bromeliaceae flowers retain conspicuous 3+3 perianth architecture and specialized absorptive leaf scales. Sedges reduce flowers into scale-subtended spikelets with nutlets; rushes have 6 tepals but lack the bromeliad rosette/trichome/seed package.

comparisons.title: Tillandsia vs Hechtia
comparisons.rule: Project Tillandsia: epiphytic, entire leaf margins, bisexual flowers, plumose seed appendages. Hechtia: terrestrial/lithophytic, spinose margins, functionally unisexual flowers on separate plants, seeds without plumose appendages.

visual_lesson.caveat: Ovary position varies across Bromeliaceae, so do not make superior or inferior ovary a universal family rule. Also do not call Tillandsia parasitic: it uses the host mainly as support.

genera.fast_cue: gray-scaled epiphyte + entire margins + bisexual 3+3 flower + plumose-seeded capsule
spinose terrestrial/lithophytic rosette + separate male/female plants + capsule

taxonomy_reconciliation.note: Accepted; native range is southwestern Texas to northeastern Mexico. Strict Hays-area range treatment remains a species-workflow question.
